12590:
A potion is a liquid that you drink, or sometimes apply to your body, to produce a special or powerful effect. That effect could be healing, harming, transforming, or even something magical — but the key idea is that the liquid does something beyond simply quenching thirst or providing nutrition.

Think of it this way: water is just a liquid. A potion is a liquid with a mission.

For a liquid to be called a potion, it generally has these qualities:

1. It is deliberately made.
A potion is not a naturally occurring liquid like river water or juice from a fruit. It is something that has been carefully prepared or mixed — usually by combining ingredients — with a specific purpose in mind. A witch brewing herbs, roots, and mysterious ingredients in a cauldron is making a potion. A pharmacist mixing compounds for a medicine can also be said to be making a potion (in a more old-fashioned or literary sense).

2. It has a specific, intended effect.
This is the most important quality. A potion does something to whoever drinks or uses it. The effect can be:

  • Healing — curing illness, closing wounds, restoring energy
  • Harmful — poisoning someone, causing illness or death
  • Magical or transformative — making someone fall in love, causing sleep, granting strength, making someone invisible, turning a person into an animal, etc.
  • Medicinal — treating a disease or symptom (used in older or more literary language)

3. It is a liquid.
A potion is always in liquid form. It is not a pill, a powder, or a spell — it is something you drink or apply. This is non-negotiable. If it's not a liquid, it's simply not a potion.
The "Feel" of the Word — Its Connotation

The word potion carries a very specific atmosphere with it. When you hear it, it tends to evoke images of:

  • Mystery and magic — dark forest huts, glowing vials, cauldrons, wizards, witches, alchemists
  • Secrecy — potions are often hidden, smuggled, or known only to their maker
  • Power — something beyond the ordinary

Because of this, the word has a slightly dramatic, old-fashioned, or fantastical tone. It is not the word you'd use casually. You wouldn't say, "I drank a potion of orange juice this morning." But you might say it humorously or metaphorically: "This coffee is my morning potion" — and that works because you're deliberately playing with that dramatic, magical quality of the word.

In everyday modern language, we usually say medicine, drug, drink, or remedy. The word potion is reserved for contexts where a sense of mystery, magic, or drama is present — either genuinely (in fantasy) or humorously.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

In fairy tales and folklore:
Potions appear constantly in traditional stories. The villain gives the hero a sleeping potion, a poison potion, or a love potion. These are central tools of magic in storytelling traditions around the world.

In fantasy fiction, movies, and games:
This is where the word is most alive today. In stories like Harry Potter, characters study potion-making as a subject, brewing liquids that heal, harm, transform, or enchant. In role-playing video games, you frequently pick up health potions (to restore life) or mana potions (to restore magical energy). Characters in fantasy novels carry small glass vials of potions into battle.

In historical and old-fashioned contexts:
Before modern medicine, healers, apothecaries (early pharmacists), and herbalists prepared liquid remedies from plants and minerals. These were often called potions. So in a historical novel set in medieval times, a healer might offer a patient a potion for the fever.

In metaphorical and humorous use:
People sometimes call any powerful, mysterious, or strongly effective liquid a potion, with a wink. A very strong cocktail, an unusual herbal tea, or a particularly effective energy drink might be called a potion in playful speech or writing.
Common Types of Potions You Should Know

• Love potion — a liquid that supposedly makes the person who drinks it fall in love, usually with a specific person. Also historically called a philter or philtre.
  • Healing potion — restores health, cures injury or disease.
  • Sleeping potion — causes deep, unnatural sleep. (Think of the apple in Snow White — the poisoned apple functioned like a sleeping potion in liquid-adjacent form.)
  • Poison potion — a liquid intended to harm or kill.
  • Strength potion / power potion — grants unusual physical or magical power temporarily.
  • Invisibility potion — causes the drinker to become invisible.
  • Truth potion — forces the drinker to tell the truth (a well-known fictional concept).
  • Transformation potion — changes the drinker's form, turning them into an animal or another person.

• The old wizard handed her a small blue potion and told her to drink it before midnight.
  • The villain slipped a sleeping potion into the knight's drink.
  • In the game, you should always carry at least three health potions before entering the dungeon.
  • She was convinced the herbalist's potion had cured her cold.
  • He jokingly called his grandmother's homemade ginger tea a "potion."

A potion is a specially prepared liquid — real or magical — that is drunk or applied to the body in order to produce a specific powerful effect, and the word carries a strong sense of mystery, magic, or old-world drama with it.
12591: Potluck has two related meanings — one concrete (about a meal), and one broader (about chance). Understanding both will give you the full picture.
Meaning 1: A shared meal where everyone brings food

This is the most common meaning today.

A potluck is a meal or gathering where each person invited brings one dish of food, and together all the dishes form the entire meal. No single person — not even the host — is responsible for cooking everything. Instead, the food "comes together" from all the guests.

Think of it this way: Imagine you're invited to a friend's home for dinner. Your friend tells you it's a potluck. This means: you're expected to bring something — maybe a salad, a dessert, a bowl of rice, or a curry. Everyone else coming will also bring something. When you all arrive, all the dishes are laid out together, and everyone eats from everything. The meal is a collective effort.

"She organized a potluck for her colleagues, and people brought everything from pasta salads to homemade pies."

Key features of a potluck:

  • Everyone contributes food — no one person does all the cooking.
  • It's usually a casual, relaxed kind of gathering.
  • The host might coordinate who brings what (to avoid five people showing up with bread), or it might be completely unplanned.
  • It is very common at office parties, community events, religious gatherings, and informal get-togethers among friends.

As a compound noun, "potluck" often appears in phrases like:

  • a potluck dinner — a dinner organized in this shared style
  • a potluck lunch / potluck supper — the same idea at lunch or supper
  • a potluck party — a party where the food is contributed by guests
Meaning 2: Whatever happens to be available — no guarantees

This is an older and slightly less common sense, but still very much in use — especially in the phrase "take potluck."

Here, potluck refers to whatever is on hand or whatever chance provides — without any special preparation or guarantee of quality. When you "take potluck," you accept whatever is available, not knowing in advance what you'll get.

"You're welcome to join us for dinner, but you'll have to take potluck — I haven't had time to cook anything special."

This means: "You can eat with us, but I can't promise a proper meal — it'll just be whatever we happen to have."

"We showed up at the hotel without a reservation, hoping to take potluck on a room."

This means: "We came without a booking and simply accepted whatever room, if any, happened to be free."

In this sense, potluck carries the idea of leaving things to chance — you don't control what you get; you just accept whatever turns up. It could be great, or it could be ordinary. You don't know.

They're really two sides of the same idea. In the "shared meal" sense, no one knows exactly what the full meal will look like until everyone arrives with their dishes — you're taking a chance on what ends up on the table. In the "whatever's available" sense, you're similarly leaving the outcome to chance. Both meanings share the spirit of accepting what comes, rather than planning and controlling every detail.
A note on tone and register

Potluck (in both meanings) is an informal word. You'd use it comfortably with friends, family, or colleagues in casual settings. You would not use it in a formal or professional document. In formal contexts, you might instead say a communal meal, a shared meal, or a cooperative dinner.

Meaning 1A gathering or meal where every guest brings a dish of food to share.
Meaning 2Whatever happens to be available; something accepted without knowing in advance what you'll get.
Common phraseTake potluck — to accept whatever is available or left to chance.

Both meanings carry the same underlying spirit: you don't control the outcome; you accept what comes.
12592: Potpourri has two meanings — one concrete and one figurative. Both are equally valid and in common use. Understanding both will give you the complete picture of this word.
The Literal Meaning — A Physical, Fragrant Mixture

In its most original, concrete sense, potpourri is a decorative mixture of dried flower petals, herbs, spices, and plant materials, placed together in an open bowl, a jar, or a small fabric pouch. The sole purpose is to make a room smell pleasant — think of it as a natural, old-fashioned air freshener.

Typical ingredients include dried rose petals, lavender, cinnamon sticks, cloves, orange peel, and cedarwood chips. Sometimes a few drops of scented oil are added to boost the fragrance. The mixture is left out in the open so its scent slowly drifts into the surrounding air.

You would commonly find a bowl of potpourri sitting on a bathroom shelf, a coffee table, inside a wardrobe, or in a hotel lobby. It serves a double purpose — it smells good, and it also looks visually appealing because of the colorful mix of dried petals and spices.

A simple way to picture it: imagine someone collects rose petals from their garden, lets them dry in the sun, then tosses them in a bowl with some cinnamon sticks and dried lavender. That fragrant, colorful bowl is potpourri.
The Figurative Meaning — A Mixed Collection of Different Things

This is the more widely used meaning of the word, and you will encounter it far more often in books, articles, and everyday speech.

When used figuratively, potpourri means a miscellaneous assortment or mixture of many different, varied things gathered together in one place — things that may not share a single strong theme but are presented as a collection. The idea is borrowed directly from the physical object: just as a bowl of potpourri blends many different ingredients, a figurative potpourri blends many different elements.

Here are some clear examples of this meaning in use:

  • A television variety show that mixes comedy skits, musical performances, cooking segments, and celebrity interviews could be described as "a potpourri of entertainment."
  • A book containing short stories, travel essays, poems, and personal memoirs on different subjects might be called "a literary potpourri."
  • If a professor's lecture jumps from ancient history, to modern politics, to pop culture, a student might say, "Today's class was a real potpourri of ideas."
  • A music album that blends jazz, classical, folk, and electronic sounds is often described as "a potpourri of musical styles."

In every case, the word signals: "There are many different things here, and they are mixed together."
The Tone and Feeling the Word Carries

This is important to understand, because not all words that mean "a mixture" feel the same.

Potpourri carries a neutral-to-pleasant tone. The variety it describes is generally seen as interesting, rich, or even charming — not messy or chaotic. When someone calls something a potpourri, they are not criticizing the mix. They are simply acknowledging the variety, often with a hint of appreciation.

Compare this to similar words:

  • Hodgepodge — suggests a clumsy, random, somewhat messy mixture, often used critically.
  • Jumble — implies disorder and confusion.
  • Medley — similar in feel to potpourri, but used almost exclusively for music or food.
  • Potpourri — refined, pleasant, and variety-embracing in tone. It can be used in formal writing or casual speech without sounding negative.

So if a writer calls a book a "potpourri of essays," they are saying it covers many topics, and the variety itself is part of the appeal. If they called it a "hodgepodge," they might be suggesting it feels disorganized.
How Broad the Figurative Use Is

The figurative meaning of potpourri is extremely flexible. It can be applied to almost anything that consists of varied, mixed elements:

  • A playlist of songs from different genres
  • A buffet with cuisines from many different countries
  • A museum exhibition covering unrelated artists from different eras
  • A conversation that jumped between sports, politics, cooking, and childhood memories
  • A gift basket filled with chocolates, candles, books, and bath products

In all these cases, the word simply signals that there is a pleasing or notable variety — a mix of things that don't all belong to one neat category.
Knowing When Each Meaning Is Intended

Context almost always makes it clear. If someone says, "I bought some potpourri for the bathroom," they mean the physical, fragrant product. If they say, "The festival was a potpourri of art, music, and culture," they mean the figurative mixture. Because the word is most commonly encountered in its figurative sense in writing and speech, that is the meaning you should default to when you are unsure.

Potpourri is a noun with two connected meanings. First, it is a physical product — a mixture of dried flowers, herbs, and spices kept in a bowl or pouch to make a space smell good. Second, and more commonly, it is used to describe any pleasant or interesting mixture of varied, diverse things — topics, styles, ideas, or items — gathered together in one place. The word carries a warm, positive tone and celebrates variety rather than criticizing it.
12593:
A potsherd is a broken piece or fragment of pottery — a chunk that has snapped, chipped, or cracked off from a clay vessel like a pot, jar, bowl, jug, or vase.

Think of it this way: if you drop a ceramic mug on the floor and it shatters, each of those broken pieces lying on the floor is a potsherd. The whole mug is pottery. The broken bits are potsherds.

That's really the heart of it — a potsherd is always a fragment, never a whole object.
What a Potsherd Actually Looks Like

Potsherds are typically rough and irregular in shape, with sharp or jagged edges where the break occurred. They can range from tiny chips the size of a coin to larger curved pieces that clearly show the shape of the original vessel. If you pick one up, you'd notice:

  • One side is often smooth or decorated (the outer or inner surface of the pot).
  • The other side (the broken cross-section) is rough and dull, showing the raw clay material.
  • The thickness and color of that raw clay edge can tell experts a great deal about how and where the pot was made.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

1. Archaeology (the most important context)

This is where the word truly lives. Potsherds are, without exaggeration, the most common object found at archaeological dig sites around the world. Here's why that matters:

Pottery has been made by humans for thousands of years. When a pot broke in ancient times, people didn't really have a way to recycle the pieces — so the fragments just stayed wherever they fell, got buried under layers of soil over centuries, and survived. Clay is extremely durable. It doesn't rot, rust, or decompose the way wood, cloth, or metal does. This means archaeologists routinely dig up potsherds that are thousands of years old — still intact, still readable.

Because of this, potsherds have become one of archaeology's most powerful tools. Here's how:

  • Dating a site: Pottery styles, shapes, and decorations changed significantly over different time periods and in different cultures. By examining a potsherd — its design, the clay used, the technique — an expert can often estimate when it was made with impressive accuracy. If you know when the potsherd was made, you know roughly when that layer of the site was in use.
  • Understanding trade: If a potsherd found in Greece is made from clay that only exists in Egypt, that's direct physical evidence of ancient trade between the two places.
  • Learning about daily life: The size and shape of a fragment can hint at what the original vessel was used for — storing grain, carrying water, cooking food, holding wine, etc.

So if you ever read about an archaeological dig, the phrase "thousands of potsherds were recovered" is not surprising at all — it's completely standard.

2. The Bible and Religious Literature

The word potsherd appears several times in the Bible, particularly in the Old Testament, often as a symbol of something broken, worthless, or humbled. For instance, in the Book of Job, the suffering Job scrapes his sores with a potsherd — a vivid image of his despair and degradation. In the Psalms and Proverbs, potsherds are used as metaphors for frailty. So if you are reading older religious or literary texts, you will encounter this word in a symbolic sense — it represents brokenness, lowliness, or something that has been reduced to rubble.

3. Ancient Writing Surfaces

Here is a fascinating use of potsherds that most people don't know about: in the ancient world, smooth potsherds were regularly used as informal writing surfaces — essentially functioning as ancient scratch paper or sticky notes.

Papyrus (the ancient equivalent of paper) was expensive and precious. For everyday notes, shopping lists, letters, receipts, and school exercises, ordinary people would simply write on a potsherd with ink. These inscribed potsherds are called ostraca (singular: ostracon, from the Greek word for shell or pottery). Thousands of ostraca have been found in ancient Egypt, Greece, Israel, and other regions, and they give historians an incredibly personal and informal window into everyday life — written in ordinary people's handwriting, about ordinary things.

4. Ancient Athenian Democracy — "Ostracism"

One of the most historically significant uses of potsherds was in ancient Athens. Citizens used them as voting ballots in a practice called ostracism. When Athenians felt that a particular person was becoming too powerful or dangerous to democracy, they held a vote. Each citizen would scratch or paint the name of the person they wanted expelled onto a potsherd and deposit it. If enough votes (at least 6,000) named the same person, that individual was banished from Athens for ten years — not as a criminal punishment, but as a political safeguard. The word "ostracism" itself comes directly from ostracon, meaning potsherd. Many such voting potsherds have been discovered by archaeologists, still bearing the scratched names of prominent Athenian politicians.

It's worth clarifying one thing: potsherd specifically refers to fragments of fired clay pottery. It does not refer to broken glass, broken stone, or broken metal — even though those fragments might be called "shards." The word sherd (or shard) is the more general term for a broken fragment of any brittle material, while potsherd is specifically about pottery.

Also note: you may occasionally see it spelled "potshard" — this is an accepted variant spelling, and you can treat the two as interchangeable.

• The museum display showed a reconstructed ancient amphora assembled from dozens of potsherds.
  • Archaeologists at the site catalogued over two thousand potsherds, most of them from the Bronze Age.
  • A single potsherd bearing a painted geometric pattern was enough for the expert to identify the vessel as Mycenaean Greek.
  • Job sat among the ashes, using a potsherd to scrape his wounds.
  • Citizens inscribed their chosen name onto a potsherd and cast their vote to ostracize the general.
A potsherd is a broken fragment of a clay pot or pottery vessel — humble in appearance, but extraordinarily valuable to archaeologists, historians, and anyone seeking to understand the ancient world.
12594: A potshot is a quick, careless, and often unfair attack — either a literal shot fired without proper aim, or a criticism thrown at someone casually and from a position of safety.

1. A physical shot (the literal meaning)

Originally, a potshot was a shot taken at an animal simply to get food for the cooking pot — not for sport, not skillfully, just a quick and easy kill. There was no challenge, no sportsmanship, no effort. Over time, the word extended to mean any random, careless shot at a person or target — one that requires little skill and is taken opportunistically, without careful aim.

"Gunmen hiding on the rooftops took potshots at people crossing the street below."

The key idea: the shot is easy, quick, and opportunistic.

2. A verbal criticism or attack (the figurative meaning — by far the most common today)

When people use the word potshot today, they almost always mean a verbal jab: a quick criticism or remark directed at someone, without a proper or fair argument behind it. It's not a careful, reasoned critique. It's a cheap dig — often made when the target isn't there to respond, isn't expecting it, or can't easily fight back.

Think of it this way: imagine someone who stands at a safe distance and throws a stone at you when you're not looking. They take no real risk. They put in no real effort. And they don't stay to face you. That's the spirit of a potshot.

"The opposition kept taking potshots at the government's policy without offering any solutions of their own."

"During the interview, he couldn't resist taking a potshot at his former boss."

"Critics lined up to take potshots at the director's new film before it was even released."
What exactly makes something a potshot?

A remark or attack earns the label potshot when it has one or more of these qualities:

  • It's quick and offhand — not a serious, developed argument, just a passing jab.
  • It's opportunistic — the attacker picks an easy moment when the target is vulnerable, absent, or in no position to respond.
  • It's often unfair — the person doesn't engage fully with the subject; they just make a cheap point and move on.
  • The attacker is in a safe position — they're throwing a punch from a distance, without putting themselves at real risk.
  • It's shallow — a potshot doesn't make a thorough case; it just scores a quick, easy hit.

None of these qualities need to all be present at the same time. Even one or two of them can make a criticism feel like a potshot.

You will almost always see potshot used with the verb take:

  • "to take a potshot at someone/something"

This is the standard phrase. You take a potshot at a person, a company, a policy, an idea — anything you're criticizing in that quick, cheap, unfair way.

You can also use it in the plural:

  • "to take potshots at someone"

When multiple people — or one person repeatedly — keep throwing quick jabs at a target, they are taking potshots. It suggests a kind of pile-on or repeated cheap targeting.
Connotation — is a potshot always negative?

Yes, almost always. Here's the important thing: when you call something a potshot, you are criticizing the attacker's behavior, not necessarily defending the target.

Saying "She took a potshot at the minister" implies:

  • Her criticism was cheap or opportunistic
  • She didn't make a full, fair argument
  • She had an unfair advantage in the moment

Even if the minister deserved criticism, calling the remark a potshot suggests it was delivered in an unfair or lazy way. It frames the attacker as someone who wasn't willing to engage properly.
Everyday situations where you'd use this word

• A politician who mocks a rival during a speech but without making a real argument — that's a potshot.
  • A reviewer who dismisses a book with a sarcastic one-liner instead of engaging with it — that's a potshot.
  • A colleague who makes a snide remark about your project in a meeting when you're not there to respond — that's a potshot.
  • Someone at a party who jokes at another person's expense when they can't defend themselves — that's a potshot.
A potshot is a quick, casual, and often unfair criticism or attack — one that is opportunistic, shallow, and usually made from a position where the attacker has little to lose.
12595: A potter is a person who makes objects out of clay — things like bowls, cups, plates, mugs, vases, pots, and decorative pieces. These clay objects, once shaped and hardened, are called pottery or ceramics. So a potter is simply the maker of pottery.

Clay in its natural state is soft, wet, and easy to shape. A potter takes this raw clay and forms it into useful or beautiful objects using their hands, simple tools, and often a device called a potter's wheel — a flat, spinning disc on which the potter places a lump of wet clay and shapes it as it spins. This technique is called throwing (as in, "throwing a pot on the wheel").

Once the object is shaped, it needs to dry and then be baked at very high temperatures in a special oven called a kiln. This process is called firing, and it transforms the soft clay into a hard, durable object. Potters often also apply a glassy coating called a glaze before the final firing, which makes the object smooth, waterproof, and often colourful.
A potter's work: functional vs. decorative

A potter can make two kinds of things:

  • Functional pottery — objects meant to be used in everyday life. Think of the mug you drink tea from, the bowl you eat cereal in, a plate, a jug, a plant pot, or a storage jar. These are practical items.
  • Decorative pottery — objects made purely for beauty, display, or artistic expression. A sculpted vase with intricate patterns, a painted ceramic tile, or a clay figurine.

Many potters make both. In fact, one of the beautiful things about pottery is that something can be both useful and beautiful at the same time — a handmade bowl, for example, can be a piece of art that you also eat your soup from.
Potter as a craft and as a profession

Pottery is one of the oldest crafts in human history, so potters have existed for thousands of years. Traditionally, a potter was a craftsperson — someone trained in a practical skill, often passing it down through generations. They made everyday items that ordinary people needed: cooking pots, storage vessels, water jars.

Today, a potter can be:

  • A studio potter or craft potter — an individual artist who works alone (or with a small team) in their own workshop, making handmade pieces, often selling them directly or through galleries.
  • A production potter — someone who makes pottery in larger quantities, often repeating the same designs efficiently.
  • An art potter — someone who thinks of their clay work more as fine art than craft, creating expressive, sometimes abstract pieces.
  • A ceramic artist — a more modern term that some potters prefer, especially when their work is more artistic. (Note: "ceramic artist" and "potter" overlap greatly, but some artists prefer "ceramic artist" to emphasise the artistic rather than the purely practical nature of their work.)
What makes a potter different from a sculptor?

Both potters and sculptors work with clay, so this is a fair question. The distinction is loose and blurry, but generally:

  • A potter focuses on vessels — hollow objects that can hold or contain things (bowls, pots, vases). Their work is rooted in function and utility, even if it's also beautiful.
  • A sculptor focuses on solid three-dimensional forms, often figures, abstract shapes, or purely artistic objects, without any concern for utility.

That said, many modern artists blur this line completely, and the word "potter" today is used broadly to mean anyone who works with clay in a craft tradition.

You'll frequently encounter "Potter" as a family name (surname). People inherit this surname because their ancestors were potters — it was a common practice in many cultures to name families after the trade they practiced. The most famous example in popular culture is Harry Potter, the fictional character from J.K. Rowling's books. When you see "Potter" used as someone's last name, it has no special meaning — it's simply a name.

• "She trained under a master potter in Japan and learned the ancient art of throwing pots."
  • "The potter carefully trimmed the base of the bowl before placing it in the kiln."
  • "My neighbour is a potter — her studio is full of beautiful hand-thrown mugs and vases."
  • "He became a professional potter after leaving his office job, and he now sells his work at craft fairs."
  • "The village potter used to supply the whole community with cooking vessels and storage pots."
The key idea to hold in your mind

If you want to remember just one thing: a potter is a person who shapes clay into objects and bakes them hard. Everything else — the wheel, the kiln, the glaze, the difference between functional and decorative, the various types of potters — is just the fuller picture around that simple core idea.
12596: The word pouf has several distinct meanings — in furniture, hairstyles, fashion, and informal British speech. Here is each one explained clearly.
1. A piece of furniture (the most common meaning today)

A pouf is a large, soft, stuffed cushion that sits directly on the floor and is used as a seat or footrest. It has no legs, no back, and no armrests.

Picture a giant, firm pillow — big enough to sit on comfortably, or to prop your tired feet up on after a long day. Poufs are typically round or square, and they come in many fabrics and colors, making them popular in living rooms and bedrooms as casual extra seating or as a footstool in front of a sofa.

"She dragged the pouf closer to the couch and rested her legs on it."

How it differs from an ottoman: People sometimes use these words interchangeably, but a traditional ottoman is usually firmer, taller, has a more rigid structure, and often has legs. A pouf, on the other hand, tends to be softer, lower to the ground, and more relaxed in feel. You will sometimes see it spelled pouffe (especially in British English) — same thing, just a different spelling.

A pouf is a way of arranging hair so that it is lifted, puffed up, or gathered into a rounded, voluminous shape — usually at the top or back of the head.

Historically, in the 18th century, poufs were dramatically tall, elaborate hairstyles worn by wealthy European women. Hair was piled high and decorated with feathers, ribbons, lace, and even miniature sculptures or model ships. These were a statement of status and fashion — some rose a foot or more above the head.

In modern everyday usage, a pouf is far simpler. It usually refers to a small section of hair at the crown of the head that is teased or back-combed upward to create a bit of height and a rounded puff shape, then pinned in place.

"She teased the front of her hair into a pouf before tying the rest up in a bun."

The key idea across both old and new uses: hair lifted and shaped into a rounded, puffy bump.
3. A puffed section of fabric in clothing

In fashion and dressmaking, a pouf refers to a section of fabric that is gathered or bunched up to create a full, rounded, balloon-like shape rather than lying flat.

You see this most often in:

  • Skirts — a "pouf skirt" (also called a bubble skirt) billows outward in a rounded dome shape, often cinching back in near the hem.
  • Sleeves — fabric gathered at the shoulder to create a puffy, rounded effect.
  • The back of a gown — fabric piled or bunched at the rear for a dramatic, voluminous look.

"Her wedding dress had a beautiful pouf at the back that fanned out across the floor."

The connecting idea here is the same as the hairstyle: something puffed up and rounded, full of air or volume.

A bath pouf (sometimes spelled bath puff) is a fluffy, net-like sponge used in the shower or bath. It is made of soft mesh netting looped and bunched together into a ball shape. You squeeze body wash or soap onto it and use it to lather and scrub your skin.

"She hung her bath pouf on the shower hook after use."

This is a more casual and commercial use of the word, largely driven by the product's puffy, rounded appearance.
5. British informal slang (offensive — know it, don't use it)

In British English, pouf (also spelled poof) is used informally and offensively as a derogatory word for a gay man. It is a slur — disrespectful and hurtful. You should be aware it exists so that if you encounter it in writing or speech, you understand what it means and the tone in which it is being used. It is not a word to use yourself.

Look across these meanings and you'll notice a pattern: nearly all of them share the idea of something soft, rounded, puffed up, or full of volume — whether it's a cushioned seat, lifted hair, ballooned fabric, or a fluffy sponge. Even the word itself sounds soft and airy. The offensive slang meaning is the outlier — it has no connection to this idea and simply developed separately in informal British speech.
Which meaning will you encounter most?

In everyday modern English — especially in home décor, interior design, and shopping — the furniture meaning (the floor cushion) is overwhelmingly the most common. If someone says "I bought a pouf for my living room," they are almost certainly talking about that. The hairstyle meaning comes up in fashion and beauty contexts. The fabric meaning comes up in clothing design. The bath pouf is common in product descriptions. The British slang is something to recognize, not use.
12597:
A poultice is a soft, moist, paste-like mass that you spread onto the skin — or onto a cloth pressed against the skin — and leave there for a period of time to treat a medical problem. It is always used externally. You never swallow a poultice; it works by sitting in direct contact with your skin.

Think of it like a medicinal mud pack that does a job on your body from the outside.
What it looks like and feels like

A poultice is wet, soft, and thick — roughly the consistency of a thick oatmeal porridge or wet clay. It is neither a dry powder nor a runny liquid. That moisture is crucial: the wetness allows the active ingredients to stay in close, continuous contact with the skin and penetrate into it over time.

It is usually warm when applied, because warmth improves blood flow to the area and helps the body heal faster — though cold poultices exist too, for reducing swelling.
What a poultice is made of

There is no single recipe. Poultices have been made from an enormous variety of substances, both in traditional home remedies and in more formal medical settings. Common materials include:

  • Bread — A classic household remedy. Wet bread was pressed onto an infected area or a wound with a splinter to draw out the foreign object or infection.
  • Mustard — Ground mustard seeds mixed with water form a sharp, warming poultice applied to the chest to ease congestion and respiratory discomfort (a mustard poultice or mustard plaster).
  • Clay or mud — Applied to insect stings, bites, and inflamed skin to cool the area and draw out irritants.
  • Activated charcoal — Mixed with water and used to draw out toxins, poisons, or deep infections from a wound.
  • Herbs — Comfrey leaves, plantain leaves, and many other plants have long been mashed or boiled and applied as poultices for bruises, sprains, and skin inflammation.
  • Flaxseed (linseed) — Boiled and mashed, then used as a warm, soothing poultice for inflammation and pain.
  • Bran, oatmeal, or other grains — Moistened and applied to soothe irritated or inflamed skin.

What all these share is that they are mixed with water or another liquid to create that characteristic wet, soft mass.
What a poultice does — its purpose

A poultice serves several different therapeutic functions depending on what it is made of and what condition it is being used for:

  1. Drawing out — Some poultices work by pulling things out of the body. A bread or charcoal poultice can help draw out pus from a boil or abscess, or help bring a splinter or thorn to the surface of the skin so it can be removed. This drawing action happens slowly, over several hours.
  2. Reducing inflammation and swelling — Poultices made from certain herbs or clay can calm inflamed tissue, reduce redness, and bring swelling down.
  3. Providing pain relief — The warmth of a poultice relaxes tense or painful muscles and joints, reducing aching. A mustard poultice applied to the back or chest, for example, creates a deep, penetrating warmth.
  4. Treating skin infections — By keeping the area moist and delivering antibacterial or antimicrobial substances directly to the skin, some poultices help fight local infections.
  5. Soothing and softening — A poultice can simply soften hardened or inflamed skin, making the area more comfortable and easier to treat further.

The method is straightforward:

  • The paste is either spread directly onto the skin or first spread onto a clean cloth (linen, muslin, gauze, or a similar material).
  • It is then placed onto the affected area of the body — a wound, a swollen joint, a congested chest, an infected boil, a sprained ankle, etc.
  • A second cloth or bandage is often placed over the top to hold it in place, retain the moisture and heat, and protect clothing.
  • It is left there — sometimes for an hour, sometimes for several hours, sometimes overnight — while it does its work.
  • Once the time is up, it is removed and the skin is cleaned.

A single application may be done once, or the poultice may be replaced with a fresh one several times a day over multiple days.
Poultices in context: when and where they appear

Poultices are one of humanity's oldest forms of medicine. Before pharmacies and modern drugs, people reached for whatever plants, food, or minerals were around them to make poultices and treat injuries and illnesses. The practice appears across virtually every culture in history.

Today, you will encounter the word in several settings:

  • Historical and literary texts — Poultices appear frequently in older novels, medical writings, and historical accounts. When a 19th-century character has a wound or a fever and someone applies something warm to their body, it is often a poultice.
  • Traditional and herbal medicine — Herbalists and practitioners of traditional medicine still use poultices as part of their treatment methods.
  • Veterinary medicine — Poultices are commonly used on horses. A hoof poultice is applied to a horse's hoof to draw out infection or to treat a bruised sole. You will see this term often if you read anything about equestrian care.
  • Occasional modern use — While most people today reach for antiseptic cream or a doctor's prescription, some people still make or use simple poultices at home as a first response to bee stings, splinters, or minor infections.
How a poultice differs from similar things

It helps to know where a poultice ends and where other similar treatments begin:

  • Ointment or cream — These are rubbed into the skin and absorbed. A poultice is not rubbed in; it sits on top of the skin as a mass and works by prolonged contact. A poultice is also far wetter and bulkier.
  • Compress — A compress is simply a cloth soaked in liquid (hot or cold water, or an herbal solution) and pressed against the skin. It contains no paste or mass of material — it is just a wet cloth. A poultice has actual substance to it.
  • Plaster (in the old-fashioned medical sense) — A plaster was similar to a poultice but usually stiffer, drier, and coated onto a backing material that was then pressed onto the skin. The mustard plaster is a classic example. The line between a poultice and a plaster is blurry, and the two terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but a poultice tends to be softer and wetter.
  • Patch or medicated dressing — These are modern, manufactured products with specific measured doses of medicine. A poultice is usually homemade, imprecise, and natural in origin.

Like many medical words, "poultice" sometimes appears in a non-medical sense, used as a metaphor. Writers and speakers occasionally use it to describe something that offers temporary comfort or relief to a problem without fully solving it — a soothing but incomplete remedy.

For example: "Aid money was only a poultice on a much deeper wound." Here, the word captures the idea that a poultice treats symptoms from the outside rather than curing the root cause. This figurative use is relatively uncommon but worth recognising when you encounter it.

A poultice is a soft, moist, medicinal paste applied to the skin and held there — usually with a cloth — to draw out infection, reduce inflammation, relieve pain, or treat a local ailment. It can be made from a wide range of substances including bread, mustard, clay, charcoal, or herbs. It is one of the oldest forms of medical treatment, still encountered today in traditional medicine, veterinary care, and occasionally in everyday home remedies.
12598:
To pounce means to jump at something suddenly and with force — usually to catch it, grab it, or attack it. Think of a cat sitting perfectly still, watching a mouse move across the floor, and then — in one sharp, explosive burst — leaping onto it. That sudden, forceful leap is a pounce.

The word always carries two key feelings inside it: sudden movement and purposeful intent. You never pounce by accident. There is always a target, and the action is always fast and deliberate.

In its most basic, physical sense, to pounce means to spring forward onto something — to leap at it in one swift motion.

This is most naturally used with animals:

  • A leopard pounces on a deer.
  • The kitten pounced on the ball of yarn.
  • An eagle pounces on its prey from above.

You'll notice the word almost always comes with "on" or "upon" after it. You pounce on something. That's the standard structure.

It can also describe a person doing something physically sudden:

  • The child pounced on his birthday gift the moment it appeared.
  • The police officer pounced on the suspect before he could run.

This is where pounce becomes truly rich and interesting. In everyday language, people use "pounce" far beyond physical jumping — and this figurative use is just as common, if not more so.

1. To jump eagerly on an opportunity

When something good becomes available, and someone acts on it immediately — with excitement and speed — we say they pounced on it.

  • She pounced on the discounted flight tickets the moment they were listed.
  • As soon as the position opened up, he pounced on the opportunity.

The idea here is that the person had been waiting, watching, and the moment the chance appeared, they moved fast, without hesitation — just like a predator that has been waiting for the right moment.

2. To immediately attack someone's mistake or weakness

When someone spots an error, a flaw, or a weakness in what another person said or did — and they immediately bring it up, challenge it, or criticize it — they are said to pounce on it.

  • The debate opponent pounced on every inconsistency in her argument.
  • My editor pounced on the factual error in my article.
  • The lawyer pounced on the witness's contradictory statement.

This use is common in debates, arguments, criticism, and journalism. There's a sharp, aggressive quality to it — the person isn't gently pointing something out; they're moving fast and going in hard.

3. To confront or question someone aggressively and suddenly

Sometimes, pounce is used when a person suddenly confronts or attacks another person (verbally), not just their ideas or mistakes.

  • Reporters pounced on the minister as he exited the building.
  • The moment she walked in, her colleagues pounced on her with questions.
The Hidden Feeling Inside the Word

What makes pounce special is the element of waiting and then suddenly striking. It is almost never a random action. There is something that happens before the pounce — a period of stillness, observation, or readiness — and then the explosive moment of action.

This gives the word a predatory quality, even when used figuratively. When you say someone pounced on an opportunity or on a person's mistake, you're subtly suggesting that they were ready, watching, and moved the moment the right moment came.

Compare:

  • "She took the opportunity." — neutral, matter-of-fact
  • "She pounced on the opportunity." — vivid, quick, eager, almost aggressive

The second sentence makes you feel the speed and the sharpness of the action.
Connotations: Is It Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

It depends entirely on context.

  • When talking about a predator or animal, it is simply descriptive — neither good nor bad.
  • When talking about seizing an opportunity, it is often positive or admiring — it suggests someone is sharp, quick-thinking, and decisive.
  • When talking about attacking someone's mistake or confronting someone aggressively, it often has a negative or critical tone — it can suggest unfairness, aggression, or being overly eager to attack.

So the same word can praise someone's decisiveness or criticize their aggression, purely based on how it's used.

To pounce is to move suddenly and with sharp purpose toward something or someone — whether physically jumping on it, eagerly seizing an opportunity, or aggressively attacking a flaw or mistake — always with the sense of having been ready and then striking fast.
12599:
To pour means to cause a liquid — or anything that moves like one — to flow steadily and continuously from one place to another, usually by tilting a container.

Picture yourself holding a jug of water over a glass and tilting it. The water flows down in a smooth, steady stream. That controlled, continuous flow from a source to a destination — that is the soul of "pour."

1. You pour something (you are making it flow)

Here, you are the one causing the flow. Something is being poured.

  • She poured water into the pot.
  • He poured himself a glass of orange juice.
  • Pour the sauce over the pasta.
  • The waiter poured wine into each glass.

The thing being poured is almost always a liquid, but it can also be any fine material that flows like one — sand, sugar, rice, grain.

  • She poured a cup of sugar into the bowl.
  • He poured sand into the mold.

2. Something pours on its own (no one is necessarily doing it)

Here, a liquid flows by itself in a steady, strong stream. You are simply describing the flow, not who caused it.

  • Water poured out of the broken pipe.
  • Blood poured from the wound.
  • Sweat poured down his face.
  • Sunlight poured through the windows.

The key idea in both cases is the same: a continuous, steady flow in one direction, in significant volume.

When it rains extremely heavily — so heavily that the rain seems to fall in streams rather than drops — we say it is pouring.

  • Take an umbrella. It's pouring outside.
  • It poured all afternoon and the streets flooded.
  • We were soaked because it was pouring with rain.

You might also hear "it's pouring down" or "it's pouring buckets" — both mean the same thing: very heavy rain. This is one of the most common everyday uses of the word.
People or Things Moving in Large Numbers

"Pour" is also used when a large number of people or things move somewhere continuously and in great quantity — just like a flowing liquid. The image is of a flood or stream of people.

  • Fans poured onto the pitch after the final whistle.
  • Refugees poured across the border.
  • Complaints poured in from customers.
  • Letters poured in from all over the country.
  • Money poured into the city's economy.

The idea: many things moving together, in one direction, steadily and in large amounts — like water from an open tap.
Figurative Uses: Feelings, Words, and Effort

"Pour" is also used for abstract things — emotions, words, energy, money — whenever there is a sense of giving a lot, freely and continuously. The physical image of flowing water is still there underneath.

Feelings and words flowing out freely

  • She poured out her feelings to her best friend. — She expressed everything she was feeling, openly and fully, holding nothing back.
  • He sat down and poured his heart out. — He shared everything that was troubling him, without any reservation.
  • They poured praise on the young athlete. — They gave a lot of praise, very generously.
  • She poured out everything that had been weighing on her.

The image: feelings or words flowing out like water — in large amounts, freely, without being held back.

Effort, money, and resources being given generously

  • The government poured billions into rebuilding the roads. — They invested enormous amounts of money.
  • She poured all her energy into the campaign. — She gave everything she had to it.
  • He has poured years of his life into this research.
  • They poured resources into developing the vaccine.

Here, "pour" suggests giving something in large quantities, fully and wholeheartedly.

These are fixed expressions that use "pour." Knowing them will make you much more comfortable with the word in real usage.

Pour your heart out — to tell someone all your deepest feelings and troubles, keeping nothing back.
"I called her at midnight and poured my heart out."

Pour cold water on something — to discourage an idea, or dampen someone's enthusiasm for it, by pointing out its problems.
"We were all excited about the plan, but the manager poured cold water on it immediately."

Pour oil on troubled waters — to say or do something to calm a conflict or tense situation. (Oil actually does smooth rough water — that's where this image comes from.)
"The senior diplomat tried to pour oil on troubled waters between the two countries."

Pour scorn on something — to speak about something in a way that makes clear you think it is worthless, ridiculous, or not worth taking seriously.
"Critics poured scorn on the film when it was first released."

Pour money down the drain — to waste money on something that produces no benefit at all.
"Buying that broken machine was just pouring money down the drain."

It never rains but it pours — a saying meaning: when bad things start to happen, they tend to pile up and happen all at once, rather than arriving one at a time.
"My car broke down, I lost my wallet, and now I have a cold — it never rains but it pours."

Across every single use — whether you're talking about water, rain, people, feelings, or money — "pour" always carries the same core qualities:

  • Volume — a lot of something, not just a little.
  • Continuity — it flows without stopping and starting; it keeps going.
  • Direction — it moves from one place toward another.
  • Ease — it flows freely and naturally, without resistance.

Once you feel this — the idea of something flowing in large quantities, steadily, freely — you will be able to understand "pour" in any context you encounter it.
